en_title: Who Have You Become Away From Home?
en_excerpt: A silent trap hides inside the immigration experience — and it has nothing to do with the airport.
en_meta_description: A systemic therapist on what emigration does to your emotional support network, and how to rebuild it in Ireland.
en_content:
Text written by: Aria Milioni

Systemic Therapist

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/ariaenergyhealing/

There is a silent trap inside the immigration experience.

It does not happen at the airport.

It does not happen when you say goodbye to your family.

Nor when you realise you have missed birthdays, weddings or important moments of

those who stayed behind.

It happens little by little.

So slowly that it often goes unnoticed.

Because emigrating does not mean only changing country.

It means inevitably losing a part of the system that regulated your emotional

life. And that is something few immigrants understand when they arrive.

When we lived near family, friends or the people who knew us

deeply, there was an invisible network holding up our emotional balance.

A spontaneous conversation. A Sunday lunch. An unexpected visit. A hug

with no need to put it in the calendar.

All of this helped our nervous system remember that we were safe.

When we emigrate, that network disappears.

And however many new friendships we build, there is a truth few people like to

admit:

Part of the isolation is inevitable. It does not matter how sociable you are. It does not matter

how many friends you make. It does not matter how much you love the country where you live.

There is a period, lasting months for some people and years for others, in which the

feeling of not fully belonging anywhere is part of the journey.

You no longer live the life you left behind. But you do not yet feel

completely part of the new reality either.

It is an emotional no man's land.

And it is exactly in this space that some of the greatest vulnerabilities

of the immigrant begin to appear.

The first of them is projection.

Without realising it, we start to expect new relationships to fill spaces that were once

occupied by an entire community.

We expect a partner to be best friend, therapist, family and safe harbour all at the same

time.

We expect recent friendships to have the depth of decades.

We expect people we met a few months ago to understand pain built up

over a whole lifetime.

And when that does not happen, the feeling of abandonment appears.

But often we are not suffering because of the relationship itself. We are suffering because of the

absence of the network that existed before it.

The problem is that there is a second factor that makes all of this even more intense. And it

rarely receives the attention it deserves.

The body. Especially when we talk about physical activity.

Many immigrants, especially those who came from sunny countries, go through

a drastic change of lifestyle.

Less time outdoors. Less exposure to the sun. Less movement. Fewer spontaneous

walks. Fewer in-person meet-ups. Less human contact.

And without realising it, they enter a dangerous cycle.

They feel more isolated.

They go out less. They move less.

And the less they move, the worse they feel.

What few people know is that movement is not only for losing weight or

improving physical health.

Movement is a tool for emotional regulation.

When we walk, run, train or simply put the body in

motion, we help the nervous system to process stress, anxiety, frustration and

sadness.

Physical activity acts as a kind of biological release valve.

It reduces stress levels. It improves mood. It promotes sleep. It increases the feeling of

energy.

And, perhaps most importantly for the immigrant, it creates an inner sense of stability.

Because there is something nobody tells us about immigration: not all longing is

emotional.

Sometimes what we are interpreting as missing home is exhaustion. Sometimes what looks like

deep sadness is a lack of sunlight. Sometimes what looks like an existential crisis is a

nervous system that has gone months without discharging accumulated tension.

And no, this does not mean that the pain of distance is not real.

It is.

The longing exists. The losses exist. The missed birthdays exist. The absences

exist.

But when the body is exhausted, sedentary and deprived of natural light, everything becomes bigger.

Rejection feels more painful.

Loneliness feels deeper.

Anxiety feels more intense.

Conflicts seem more serious.

Goodbyes seem more final.

That is why one of the biggest mistakes an immigrant can make is to believe that all of their

emotional challenges will be solved through the mind alone.

Analysis is essential, but it does not feed the needs of the physical body.

In the vast majority of cases, the only real need is more movement.

More walking. More nature. More fresh air. More contact with the physical world.

Especially during the long winter months.

Because winter does not affect only mood. It affects our perception of life.

For someone who grew up surrounded by sun, consecutive months of grey sky can

reduce energy, motivation and the emotional capacity to deal with challenges.

And when we add that to the inevitable isolation of immigration, the effects become even

more evident.

That is why creating a routine of movement is not a luxury. It is not vanity. It is not merely

a health matter.

It is a strategy for emotional survival.

It is a way of telling the nervous system: “We are far from home, but we are
safe.”

Perhaps the greatest lesson of immigration is realising that belonging is not born only from

the people around us.

It is also born from the relationship we build with ourselves.

And that relationship is not created through thoughts alone.

It is created through the small daily choices that help the body, the mind and the

heart to walk together.

So the next time you feel that longing is crushing your chest, ask

a simple question before concluding that something is wrong:

Are you really missing home…

Or has it been weeks since your body has been begging to get out of the chair, see daylight and

remind your nervous system that there is still life happening out there?

With love,

Aria Milioni
